question: What is the difference between vertical scaling and horizontal scaling?

key_points: Vertical scaling (scaling up): adding more resources (CPU, RAM) to a single existing machine
Horizontal scaling (scaling out): adding more machines/instances and distributing load across them
Vertical scaling is simpler (no distributed system complexity) but has a hard ceiling (max hardware spec) and creates a single point of failure
Horizontal scaling requires distributing state/load balancing but scales much further and improves fault tolerance, since losing one instance doesn't take the whole system down
reference_solution.sample_answer: Vertical scaling, or scaling up, means adding more resources — more CPU or RAM — to a single existing server. Horizontal scaling, or scaling out, means adding more server instances and distributing the load across all of them. Vertical scaling is simpler since you avoid all the complexity of a distributed system, but it has a hard ceiling — there's a maximum spec of hardware you can buy — and it leaves you with a single point of failure, since that one bigger machine going down takes everything with it. Horizontal scaling requires more upfront design work, like a load balancer and handling shared state across instances, but it scales much further in principle and improves fault tolerance, since losing any single instance doesn't take the whole system down.

follow_up_hint: Ask what architectural changes are needed to make an application horizontally scalable if it currently stores session state in local server memory.

question: What does it mean for an application to be 'stateless', and why does statelessness matter for horizontal scaling?

key_points: A stateless application server doesn't store any client-specific session data in its own memory/local disk between requests — any request can be handled by any server instance
Statelessness means any load balancer can route a given request to any healthy instance without needing 'sticky sessions' tied to a specific server

Stateful servers (storing session data locally) require either sticky sessions (limiting load balancing flexibility and fault tolerance) or externalizing that state (e.g. to Redis) to become effectively stateless from the load balancer's perspective
Enables simple, elastic horizontal scaling: instances can be added/removed freely since no instance holds unique, irreplaceable state
reference_solution.sample_answer: A stateless application server doesn't keep any client-specific data, like session information, in its own local memory or disk between requests — every request contains (or can retrieve) everything needed to process it independently. This matters for horizontal scaling because it means a load balancer can route any incoming request to any healthy server instance, since none of them are uniquely 'holding' state a particular client depends on. If a server does store session state locally, you either need sticky sessions, which tie a client to one specific instance and reduce load-balancing flexibility and fault tolerance — since losing that one instance loses that client's session — or you externalize that state to a shared store like Redis, which makes the application servers themselves effectively stateless again from the load balancer's point of view. Statelessness is what lets you freely add or remove server instances to scale elastically, since no instance is irreplaceable.

follow_up_hint: Ask them how they'd migrate an existing application using in-memory sessions to be stateless without breaking logged-in users during the migration.

question: How would you scale a database that's becoming a bottleneck as read traffic grows?

key_points: First lever for read-heavy load: add a caching layer (Redis/Memcached) in front of the database for frequently-read, less frequently-changed data
Read replicas: replicate the primary database to one or more read-only replicas, and route read queries to replicas while writes go to the primary — scales read throughput horizontally
Explains replication introduces replication lag, so reads from a replica can be slightly stale — acceptable for many use cases, but not for reads that must reflect a just-completed write
If write load (not just read load) also becomes the bottleneck, sharding/partitioning the data across multiple database instances is the next, more complex lever
reference_solution.sample_answer: For read-heavy bottlenecks, I'd first look at adding a caching layer, like Redis, in front of the database for data that's read frequently but doesn't change on every request, which can eliminate a large fraction of database hits entirely. Next, I'd add read replicas — replicating the primary database to one or more read-only copies, and routing read queries to those replicas while all writes still go to the primary — which scales read throughput close to linearly by adding more replicas. The catch is replication lag: replicas are usually slightly behind the primary, so reads from a replica can occasionally return marginally stale data, which is fine for most use cases but not for anything that needs to immediately reflect a write that just happened, like showing a user their own just-submitted comment — that specific read might need to go to the primary or use read-your-writes consistency tricks. If write throughput itself eventually becomes the bottleneck too, not just reads, the next and more complex step would be sharding the data across multiple database instances by some partition key.

follow_up_hint: Ask how they'd solve the 'read-your-own-writes' problem for a user who just posted a comment but is reading from a lagging replica.
